label: MySQL
summary: Connections against their limit, threads running, row locks, slow queries, replica lag
source: mysqld_exporter (prometheus-community), default collectors (global_status, global_variables, slave_status): collector/global_status.go, global_variables.go, slave_status.go, exporter.go and mysqld_exporter.go read at main on 2026-10-09 (v0.20.0 the latest release; it supports MySQL 5.6 and later and MariaDB 10.3 and later); the queries were not run against a live server. SHOW GLOBAL STATUS becomes mysql_global_status_<variable in lower case>, except the groups the exporter folds into labelled series (Connection_errors_* into mysql_global_status_connection_errors_total{error}), and SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES mysql_global_variables_<name>. The replica's lag is the column SHOW REPLICA STATUS calls Seconds_Behind_Source and SHOW SLAVE STATUS Seconds_Behind_Master; the exporter tries SHOW ALL SLAVES STATUS, SHOW SLAVE STATUS, then SHOW REPLICA STATUS, so MySQL 8.4, which removed SHOW SLAVE STATUS, exports mysql_slave_status_seconds_behind_source, and older MySQL and MariaDB mysql_slave_status_seconds_behind_master (MySQL 8.0.22 to 8.3 rename the column only in SHOW REPLICA STATUS's output, as MySQL worklog WL#14171 specifies: SHOW SLAVE STATUS keeps the old names; MariaDB's column is still Seconds_Behind_Master): the query reads either. A NULL lag, when replication is stopped, is skipped, so it leaves no series rather than a 0. MariaDB has every status variable these queries read under the same name (its status-variable and InnoDB status-variable references, checked the same day), and the exporter reads it the same way. MySQL permits max_connections + 1 connections (one kept for CONNECTION_ADMIN) and more on its administrative interface, so connections.used.pct can pass 100. Slow_queries counts queries longer than long_query_time whether or not the slow query log is on. Tools' names checked the same day against Telegraf's inputs.mysql (README and mysql.go: with metric_version = 2, a status variable is the field mysql.<variable in lower case>; left unset, version 1 maps some names otherwise and keeps replica columns' case), Datadog's mysql metadata.csv, const.py and conf.yaml.example, the OpenTelemetry mysqlreceiver documentation.md and the AWS/RDS metric list. Datadog sends slow queries and row lock waits as per-second rates, and its replication metrics need replication: true (on with dbm). OTel's mysql.server.healthy is not named: what makes it 0 was not checked. AWS/RDS has no MySQL-internal metric: ReplicaLag is the one named, and DatabaseConnections is a count, not a share of max_connections. A ratio of a tool's metrics is null: export the computed series under the catalogue's name.

metrics.name: up
metrics.label: Exporter can reach MySQL
metrics.description: 1 while mysqld_exporter can reach MySQL, 0 when it cannot. Any 0 during the run means the server was unreachable for at least one scrape, and every other metric is blind for that span. An exporter that goes with its target (a sidecar, a deleted pod) leaves no 0, only a gap: a short gap reads PASS, and one longer than the coverage floor allows reads LOW COVERAGE.

metrics.name: connections.used.pct
metrics.label: Connections used (% of max_connections)
metrics.description: Open connections as a percentage of max_connections, at their peak. At 100 % new connections are refused with "Too many connections". MySQL keeps one more for an administrator, so it can read just past 100.

metrics.name: connections.refused
metrics.label: Connections refused at max_connections, per minute (peak)
metrics.description: Connections MySQL refused because max_connections was reached, in any minute of the run. Those clients got errors.

otel.note: off by default: enable it under the mysql receiver's metrics; error=max_connections

metrics.name: threads.running
metrics.label: Threads running (peak)
metrics.description: Connections executing a statement rather than sleeping, at their peak. Far above the number of cores, statements queue for CPU or for each other's locks, and every query slows down.

metrics.name: row.lock.waits
metrics.label: Row lock waits per minute (peak)
metrics.description: Times an InnoDB statement had to wait for a row lock another transaction held, in any minute of the run. A count that climbs with the load means contention on hot rows, which turns into lock wait timeouts.

metrics.name: slow.queries
metrics.label: Slow queries per minute (peak)
metrics.description: Queries that took longer than long_query_time, in any minute of the run, whether or not the slow query log is on. What counts as slow is the server's setting, so compare runs on one configuration.

otel.note: off by default: enable it under the mysql receiver's metrics

metrics.name: buffer.pool.hit.pct
metrics.label: InnoDB buffer pool hit ratio (%)
metrics.description: Logical reads InnoDB served from the buffer pool rather than from disk, as a percentage, per minute. A drop under load means the working set no longer fits in memory. Weak as an absolute: compare it with a baseline run.

metrics.name: replication.lag.seconds
metrics.label: Replication lag (s)
metrics.description: How far a replica's applier is behind its source, in seconds. A write-heavy test can leave replicas serving stale reads. Reported by replicas only, and only while replication runs.

telegraf.note: needs gather_slave_status = true and metric_version = 2; MySQL 8.4 needs gather_replica_status, which names it slave_seconds_behind_source

datadog.note: needs replication: true in the MySQL check's options (on with dbm: true)

otel.note: off by default: enable it under the mysql receiver's metrics; read on the replica

cloudwatch.note: RDS read replicas; statistic Maximum, per DBInstanceIdentifier
